Languish

LANG-gwish -- from Old French languir, from Latin languere ('to be faint, weak'). · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To languish is to remain in an unpleasant or neglected state for a long time, gradually growing weaker.

Overshadowed by flashier startups, the once-promising app languished for years with barely any new users.

Worked Example

After the theater lost its funding, the beautiful old building languished for a decade, its paint peeling and its seats gathering dust.

That slow, neglected decline over a long stretch of time -- not a sudden collapse -- is exactly what it means to languish.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — langu-

root — langu-: to be faint, weak (Latin (languere))

suffix — -ish

suffix — -ish: verb ending (as in finish, vanish) (French)

Put it together

Put it together: Languish comes from Latin languere, 'to be faint or weak,' with the French verb ending -ish, as in finish and vanish -- to languish is literally to grow weak and stay that way, worn down by neglect rather than any single sudden blow.

Use the root in a new word: languor

Use the root in a new word: languor: A heavy languor settled over the household in the sticky heat of August.

Root Check

Word Choice

Languish almost always implies a long, slow decline caused by neglect -- a career, a plant, or a forgotten project all languish rather than collapse all at once.
